Fraud reports, victims and losses: three numbers that need different planning questions

Three source-backed charts explore the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre’s 2025 category tables, with a display control that preserves the original observations.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare the published fraud categories without changing their observations

Official CAFC category observations for calendar 2025, from the page issued and modified 25 February 2026, retrieved 25 October 2026. The control changes only the number of rows displayed, selecting the first N categories in the source’s reported-dollar-loss ranking. It never edits a report, victim count or loss observation. All three charts use the same selected categories; the derived-ratio chart reorders them by that ratio. Published dollar losses are rounded millions, not exact underlying claim totals. Derived ratios are rounded again to the nearest CAD 100 and are not medians, personal risk estimates or household loss forecasts. The all-category headline is a lower-bound statement, not an exact denominator for shares. Reports, source-listed victims and dollars are distinct measures; the table does not establish unique people across categories or full population coverage. No underreporting multiplier, population probability, causal effect or promised reimbursement is calculated. N/A losses in the source’s frequency table remain unavailable, not zero, and are not inserted into this dollar-loss ranking.

The central idea

A reported loss ranking can identify serious patterns. It cannot supply your personal chance of being defrauded, the typical loss of a household, or a guarantee that money will be recovered.

01

Start with the reporting system and the reference year

A financial-safety plan benefits from evidence about fraud, but a headline must be matched to the question it can answer. A reported dollar loss describes a financial amount. A report count describes entries received by a reporting system. Neither is automatically a probability for one person receiving a suspicious message.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre’s 2025 top-ten page reports more than CAD 704 million of losses and over 112,000 reports across its system. Its category tables are the controlling source for the charts here. The page was issued and modified on 25 February 2026; the observations concern calendar 2025.

The display control selects between three and ten categories from the published dollar-loss ranking. It does not change any observation or construct a household scenario. Five categories appear in the original view. The count chart keeps their dollar-loss order so that the reader can compare the same rows, while the derived-ratio chart deliberately uses its own ordering.

These are administrative reported observations, not a representative sample of every Canadian household or every encounter with a scam. The charts provide neither a population exposure count nor the total number of unreported incidents. A denominator needed for a personal victimization probability is absent.

02

Keep the loss amount, report count and victim count separate

The first chart ranks selected categories by reported dollar amount. The grouped chart places the source’s report and victim columns beside each other. Different quantities can move differently: a category with fewer listed reports can still have substantial financial losses.

Do not add report counts and victim counts together. They describe different units. Nor does a category table establish that every listed victim is a distinct person across all categories, that every report concerns one household, or that the counts represent the number of people who encountered an attempt.

The control preserves a common set of categories across all three charts. Expanding to ten reveals more of the source’s loss ranking; it does not turn the selection into the entire reporting system. The selection is by dollar loss, so it should not be presented as the ten most frequent categories or as a ranking of how likely one household is to encounter each type.

The first two bar charts begin their magnitude axes at zero. Their different units remain explicit. A long dollar-loss bar and a short count bar cannot be divided visually to obtain a precise rate; the derived calculation needs the actual values and a stated denominator.

03

A loss-per-count ratio is an average of reported aggregates

The third chart divides each rounded category loss by its listed victim count. It then rounds the result to the nearest CAD 100. That additional rounding avoids showing cents of precision unsupported by a source that publishes losses in rounded millions.

The calculation changes the question from total reported financial scale to reported loss per listed victim count. It can therefore change the category order. That is an arithmetic consequence of choosing another denominator, rather than a contradiction between charts.

The result is not a median, a typical household outcome or the cost a particular person should expect. A small number of very large losses can influence an aggregate ratio, and the table does not supply the individual loss distribution needed to inspect that effect. It also supplies no uncertainty interval for the displayed comparison.

Reported aggregates should not be treated as independent, identically exposed household observations. Reporting behaviour, category definitions and the underlying incidents can differ. The ratio is useful as a clearly named descriptive calculation, with those limitations retained, rather than as an actuarial price for an individual’s risk.

04

Preserve unavailable amounts and lower-bound headlines

The source also publishes a separate frequency table containing N/A dollar-loss entries. An unavailable amount is not the number zero. It should not become a zero-height loss bar, a claim that no harm occurred, or a zero average obtained by dividing it by a count.

This article therefore uses the source’s dollar-loss ranking for the selected loss comparisons and preserves the unavailable entries in its source extract. It does not merge the two top-ten selections into a single invented population.

The all-category loss headline says more than a stated amount. It is not an exact total with which to calculate exact category shares. Rounded category amounts add another precision limit. The article avoids a pie chart or an exact percentage of all national losses.

The Competition Bureau’s March 2026 release describes substantial underreporting. That makes the reporting-system boundary material. It does not justify multiplying every category by one assumed reporting factor or converting the published totals into a new national-loss estimate. Such a calculation would require defensible assumptions about which incidents are missing and how their losses differ.

05

Use the evidence to review a payment process

A household can use the patterns as a reason to examine how unusual requests reach its money. The practical record might identify who can approve a large transfer, how an unexpected caller is verified, and which independently obtained contact details are used to check a request.

CAFC’s fraud-investigator guidance explains that criminals may impersonate trusted investigators or financial institutions. Verify an unexpected request through a channel you obtain independently, rather than treating a caller’s claimed role or displayed number as proof. The relevant question is whether the request has been authenticated before money or account access is supplied.

CAFC’s investment-fraud guidance also supports checking a proposed investment and the people offering it. A polished page, a persuasive introduction or an apparent account balance does not itself verify an opportunity. Use the current official guidance linked below when a specific proposal needs checking; these charts do not assess an actual person or product.

The controls and reserves in a financial plan have separate roles. Access to an emergency account can help meet legitimate bills after a disruption, but it does not validate a request to move money. Keeping another account balance on a chart is not evidence that a suspicious transfer can safely be made.

06

Keep reporting, recovery and future planning distinct

Reporting an incident helps establish a record; it does not promise recovery or determine reimbursement rights. The official CAFC page links to the reporting service and advises contacting local police when fraud or cybercrime is suspected. Use those official channels and retain relevant transaction records when an actual incident occurs.

When planning after a loss, distinguish confirmed available money, disputed transactions and possible recoveries. An amount under investigation should not automatically be treated as cash for next month’s bills. Any reimbursement assumption needs its own support and payment date.

Return to the dated source when updating the article. A later release, a partial-year update and an annual table can cover different windows or classifications. Do not splice them into a trend without first checking those definitions. A change in reported totals can reflect reporting as well as the underlying harm.

The useful output of these charts is a better set of questions: which unit is being counted, which incidents are represented, how much rounding is present, and what action is supported by the evidence. Keeping those questions visible makes the statistics relevant to a household safety process without pretending they predict one person’s outcome.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first two charts reproduce selected CAFC 2025 reported category observations. The third is an original ratio derived from rounded source losses and the listed victim counts. The charts are descriptive and do not estimate the Canadian population’s fraud rate. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre · Top 10 frauds in 2025 ↗

    Issued and modified 25 February 2026; retrieved 25 October 2026. Governing source for ten reported-dollar-loss category rows, their report/victim counts, rounded losses and separately retained N/A entries. The stored extract preserves the original HTML SHA-256.

  2. Competition Bureau · Fraud Prevention Month 2026 ↗

    Release dated 6 March 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026 for underreporting and reporting context. Its narrative ranking is not substituted for the controlling CAFC category table, and no underreporting multiplier is applied.

  3. Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre · Bank investigator ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for independently checking unexpected requests and impersonation context. No current caller, claim or financial institution is assessed by this article.

  4. Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre · Investment fraud ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for checking investment offers. The guide makes no recommendation, assesses no specific offer and promises no recovery.
